newsitem.title: UK: LG Metals justifies trading, denies facing losses.
newsitem.headline: LG Metals justifies trading, denies facing losses.

text.p: LG Futures Co Ltd, broker for LG Metals Corp, has submitted to South Korea's finance ministry a document explaining why LG Metals' metal trade had surged this year.

LG Futures, an affiliate of the LG Group, had been asked on June 23 by the finance ministry to explain why its metal trade had surged this year and whether the company was facing huge options-related copper losses, as rumoured in London.

Asked on Monday if LG Metals was exposed on the London Metal Exchange (LME), Yoon Kyung-eun, General Manager of LG Futures marketing team, said: "I don't think so. One or two traders on the LME got some rumours."
The document and supporting figures, obtained by Reuters, showed metal trade on the LME by LG Metals increasing since the second half of last year.

Explaining the upsurge in futures and options trading, the document said LG Metals "needed actively to trade on the LME to hedge their physical aluminium and copper trade's risks on the volatile metal market".
The document, submitted to the finance ministry by LG Futures, gave details of the open positions of LG Metals as of March 31 and June 20.

Open positions included copper shorts of 105,475 tonnes and aluminium longs of 125,900 tonnes as of June 20. LG calculated this by multiplying net open positions with delta figures based on 0.95 of copper calls, 0.5 of copper puts, 0.05 of aluminium calls and 0.95 of aluminium puts.

However, figures submitted by LG Futures showed net open positions included short copper futures of 42,225 tonnes, short copper calls of 81,225 tonnes and short copper puts of 278,325 tonnes as of June 20.
The company also had net short aluminium futures of 134,450 tonnes, short calls of 165,950 tonnes and short puts of 610,200 tonnes as of June 20, the document showed.

LG Metals' copper physical trade for this year was estimated at 268,733 tonnes of copper concentrates, 36,873 tonnes of copper imports, 311,635 tonnes for physical sales and 78,395 tonnes of copper stocks.
Aluminium physical trade for this year was estimated at 150,000 tonnes of purchases and 150,000 tonnes of sales.

The document also said the surge in South Korea's base metals futures and options trade this year was mainly due to transferring positions and synthetic hedging strategies by LG Metals -- the public explanation given by the finance ministry on July 1.
Since early this year, LG Metals has used multiple LME brokers and different strategies to keep its open positions from being exposed, it said.
It also said when expiry dates came, the company transferred its positions from one broker to another who had opposite positions.
The document also attributed surging metal trade to its delta hedging strategy combined with options and futures trade.

As of June 20, LG Metals' open positions were estimated at about 15 percent of its copper physical trade and 42 percent of its aluminium physical trade, it said. LG Metals has had open positions within its physical trade amount for one year.
Although LG Metals has been rumoured to be facing huge open losses, its futures and options operation was within its credit lines and its letter of credit (L/C) amounts, the document said.
The rumours also have not taken into account the company's physical profits which were estimated at about $80 million this year due to strong copper prices in 1997, it said.
Yoon denied the finance ministry had requested any data on trading by LG Metals.
"The finance ministry did not request anything from LG officials about LG Metals' position," he told Reuters.
But he added: "Unofficially is different. We have a good working-level relationship."
"All our futures transactions are controlled by the finance ministry. We cannot do any over-trading," Yoon said.

Lee Jong-gap, Director of the finance ministry's financial market division, told Reuters on Monday the ministry had asked LG Futures on an unofficial basis to explain the sudden upsurge in commodities futures trading, which it had explained.

"...transferring positions among brokers by major local traders and more complicated hedging strategies which combine futures and options were the main reason behind South Korea's rising metal futures turnover," the document said.
--London newsroom 44 171 542 7726
